text: Last lesson described the landing zone pattern in the abstract. This one names Azure's real implementation: management groups, the split between platform and landing zone subscriptions, and subscription vending as the automated process that ties it all together. By the end, you'll know exactly which subscription a new workload lands in and why.

A single Azure subscription has no relationship to any other subscription on its own. Management groups fix that: they sit above subscriptions, rooted at one Tenant Root Group, and any policy or role assignment made at a management group level is inherited automatically by every subscription beneath it. The Azure Landing Zones reference architecture arranges that hierarchy into two top-level groups — Platform and Landing Zones — so a policy written once reaches every subscription under it without being reapplied by hand.

Three subscriptions typically sit under Platform, and none of them run application workloads. Identity houses domain or identity infrastructure other subscriptions depend on. Management holds centralized Log Analytics and Automation — the tooling that watches everything else. Connectivity is the hub virtual network: gateways, Azure Firewall, and centralized DNS that every other subscription peers into instead of building its own internet edge from scratch.

Landing Zones is where application teams actually deploy resources. Its Corp and Online sub-groups split workloads by connectivity need, not by technology — Corp for private, internally-facing traffic, Online for workloads that accept more direct internet exposure. Either way, a new subscription placed here inherits policy from its management group and network connectivity back to the hub automatically, without requesting its own firewall rules or circuit.

Building all of this correctly once is easy. Doing it consistently for the thirtieth subscription a team requests is the real problem, and subscription vending is the answer: a requester supplies a name, a management group, a network size, and a budget, and a pipeline produces a fully compliant subscription already peered to the hub. This is Course 8's Terraform module pattern, just applied one level up — at the subscription level instead of the resource level.

Azure solves multi-account governance with management groups, policy inheritance, and subscription vending. Next lesson covers AWS's answer to the exact same problem — Organizations, Organizational Units, and Control Tower's Account Factory — using different names for a structure you'll recognize immediately.
